cards.statement: A byte variable is assignable to a uint8 variable because they have the same type.
cards.explanation: byte is an alias for uint8, so using either spelling preserves type identity.

source.title: builtin package documentation

cards.statement: A `var label string` declaration initializes label to nil.
cards.explanation: A string's zero value is the empty string, "". Declaring a string variable with no initializer gives it that value.
cards.misconception: Strings use nil as their zero value.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification: The zero value

cards.statement: A package-level variable can use `:=` for its declaration and initializer.
cards.explanation: Short variable declarations belong inside functions. A package-level variable uses a var declaration.
cards.misconception: Short variable declarations work at package scope.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: With x declared earlier in the same block, `x, err := f()` reuses x if its type matches and err is new.
cards.explanation: A short declaration reassigns a variable declared earlier in the same block if its type stays the same and a non-blank variable is new.

source.title: Effective Go

cards.statement: The declaration `v := 1.5` gives v the type float64.
cards.explanation: An untyped floating-point constant defaults to float64 when a variable declaration supplies no explicit type.

source.title: Go Blog: Constants

cards.statement: The declaration `const n uint8 = 256` stores the wrapped value 0 in n.
cards.explanation: A typed constant's value has to fit its type. The value 256 exceeds uint8's range, so this declaration fails to compile.
cards.misconception: Typed constants wrap to fit their declared types.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Constants

cards.statement: A fresh const declaration starts its iota sequence at zero.
cards.explanation: iota tracks the position of a constant specification within its const declaration. A separate declaration starts a new sequence.

source.title: builtin package documentation

cards.statement: Assigning an int variable to an int64 variable performs an implicit numeric conversion.
cards.explanation: int and int64 are distinct types. Assigning an int variable to an int64 variable requires an explicit conversion such as int64(x).
cards.misconception: Go implicitly converts between numeric variable types.

source.title: Go FAQ

cards.statement: At run time, overflowing a signed integer wraps according to its integer representation.
cards.explanation: Signed integer operations may overflow. Their results are defined by the representation, operation and operands, and overflow does not panic.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: The compiler rejects integer division when the divisor is a variable whose value is zero.
cards.explanation: A zero-valued variable is a valid integer divisor at compile time. Executing the division with that value causes a run-time panic.
cards.misconception: A variable's zero value makes division a compile-time error.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: The gc compiler rejects an unused local variable introduced by a var declaration.
cards.explanation: The spec lets a compiler reject a local variable that is never used, and the gc toolchain does: the Go FAQ says Go refuses to compile programs with unused variables.

source.title: Go FAQ: Can I stop these complaints about my unused variable/import?

cards.statement: Since Go 1.21, `min(values...)` accepts an int slice expanded as variadic arguments.
cards.explanation: The built-in min accepts separate ordered arguments, not a slice expanded with .... A call such as min(a, b) is valid.
cards.misconception: The built-in min supports variadic slice expansion.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: A Go string can contain arbitrary bytes that form invalid UTF-8.
cards.explanation: A string stores bytes rather than enforcing a text encoding. Invalid UTF-8 byte sequences are valid string contents.

source.title: Go Blog: Strings, bytes, runes and characters in Go

cards.statement: The expression `len("é")` counts the Unicode code points in the string.
cards.explanation: len measures a string in bytes. The UTF-8 encoding of é takes two bytes, so len("é") evaluates to 2.
cards.misconception: String length counts Unicode code points.

source.title: builtin package documentation

cards.statement: Indexing a string with `s[i]` yields a value of type byte.
cards.explanation: A string index selects the byte at the given byte position. The result has type byte even when the string contains UTF-8 text.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Index expressions

cards.statement: A raw string literal interprets `\n` as a newline character.
cards.explanation: Backslashes have no escape meaning inside a raw string literal. The characters backslash and n remain literal characters.
cards.misconception: Raw string literals process backslash escapes.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: A range loop over a string uses byte offsets for its index values.
cards.explanation: The index in a string range loop points to the first byte of the current UTF-8 code point, so successive indexes need not differ by one.

source.title: Go Blog: Strings, bytes, runes and characters in Go

cards.statement: A range loop over a string skips invalid UTF-8 bytes when producing rune values.
cards.explanation: An invalid UTF-8 sequence makes string range yield U+FFFD. The next iteration advances by one byte.
cards.misconception: String range silently skips malformed UTF-8 bytes.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: Writing into `[]byte(s)` changes the corresponding byte in the original string s.
cards.explanation: Converting a string to []byte gives writable bytes. Changes to those bytes leave the original string unchanged.
cards.misconception: A string-to-byte-slice conversion shares writable string storage.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: The conversion `string(65)` produces the decimal text "65".
cards.explanation: string(65) produces "A", the UTF-8 encoding of code point 65. Integer-to-string conversion interprets the integer as a code point.
cards.misconception: Converting an integer to string formats its decimal digits.
cards.volatilityNote: The specification says this historical integer-to-string conversion may eventually be removed.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: The comparison `"Z" < "a"` uses case-insensitive alphabetic ordering.
cards.explanation: The spec compares two strings lexically byte-wise and does no case folding. 'Z' is byte 0x5A and 'a' is 0x61, so "Z" < "a" is true: every upper-case ASCII letter sorts before every lower-case one.
cards.misconception: String comparison folds letter case before ordering.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Comparison operators

cards.statement: The zero value of strings.Builder is ready to accept writes.
cards.explanation: A declared strings.Builder starts ready for use. Its Write methods build the string returned by String.

source.title: strings package documentation

cards.statement: The types `[3]int` and `[4]int` are assignable because their element types match.
cards.explanation: An array's length is part of its type. Arrays of lengths three and four have different types despite having the same element type.
cards.misconception: Matching element types make different array lengths assignable.

source.title: Go Blog: Go Slices: usage and internals

cards.statement: Assigning an array to another variable copies its elements.
cards.explanation: An array value contains its elements. Assignment copies that value, so changing one array's element leaves the other's element intact.

source.title: Go Blog: Go Slices: usage and internals

cards.statement: Two slices of the same array observe writes to their overlapping elements.
cards.explanation: Slices that overlap in an underlying array refer to the same element storage. A write through either slice is visible through the other.

source.title: Go Blog: Go Slices: usage and internals

cards.statement: With `0 <= n < c`, `make([]int, n, c)` creates a slice whose length is c.
cards.explanation: make uses length for the initial element count. capacity determines the space available in the underlying array.
cards.misconception: The capacity argument also sets a slice's initial length.

source.title: builtin package documentation

cards.statement: A valid full slice expression `s[:n:n]` makes the result's capacity equal to n.
cards.explanation: A full slice expression sets capacity to max-low. In s[:n:n], the omitted low is zero and max is n.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Slice expressions

cards.statement: Appending within a slice's existing capacity gives the result a separate underlying array.
cards.explanation: When capacity suffices, append extends the slice using its existing underlying array. The returned slice refers to that array.
cards.misconception: append allocates a separate array even when existing capacity suffices.

source.title: builtin package documentation

cards.statement: Appending an element to a nil slice produces a usable slice containing that element.
cards.explanation: append accepts a nil slice and allocates storage for the added element. Its returned slice contains the appended element.

source.title: Go Blog: Arrays, slices (and strings): The mechanics of append

cards.statement: Slices of comparable elements support comparison to another slice with `==`.
cards.explanation: Slice values support comparison with nil, but not comparison with another slice using ==. Comparable elements do not make a slice type comparable.
cards.misconception: Comparable elements make slices comparable with ==.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: The built-in copy uses the shorter source or destination length as its element count.
cards.explanation: copy transfers min(len(dst), len(src)) elements. It uses the slices' lengths to bound the transfer.

source.title: builtin package documentation

cards.statement: Assigning to a slice's range value variable replaces the corresponding slice element.
cards.explanation: A slice's range value variable holds a copy of the element. Reassigning that variable changes the copy rather than replacing the slice element.
cards.misconception: The range value acts as a writable reference to the slice element.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification

cards.statement: Since Go 1.21, `clear(s)` changes the length of a slice s to zero.
cards.explanation: clear sets a slice's elements to their zero values. The slice keeps its existing length.
cards.misconception: clear empties a slice by resetting its length.

source.title: builtin package documentation: clear

cards.statement: The size hint in `make(map[string]int, hint)` fixes the map's maximum entry count.
cards.explanation: make's map size is an initial space hint, not an entry limit. A map grows to accommodate additional entries.
cards.misconception: The size hint imposes a map's maximum number of entries.

source.title: Go Programming Language Specification: Map types

cards.statement: Looking up a string key in a nil map[string]int returns zero.
cards.explanation: A nil map[string]int contains no entries. Looking up a string key returns the zero value of int, which is 0.

source.title: Go Blog: Go maps in action

cards.statement: Assigning an entry to a nil map allocates storage for that map.
cards.explanation: Assigning to a nil map causes a run-time panic. Initialize the map with make or a map literal before adding entries.
cards.misconception: A nil map allocates storage on its first assignment.

source.title: Go Blog: Go maps in action

cards.statement: For a key k stored with value 0, `v, ok := m[k]` sets ok to true.
cards.explanation: ok reports whether key k is present in the map, whatever its element holds, so a key stored with 0 gives v == 0 and ok == true. An absent key gives false.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Index expressions

cards.statement: Calling delete with an absent map key causes a run-time panic.
cards.explanation: delete leaves the map unchanged when the specified key is absent. Removing a missing entry is a no-op.
cards.misconception: Deleting an absent key is an invalid map operation.

source.title: builtin package documentation

cards.statement: With `m := map[string]struct{ X int }{}`, the assignment `m["a"].X = 1` fails to compile.
cards.explanation: Map elements are not addressable, so a field of a struct element cannot be assigned in place. Store a whole new element with m["a"] = v, or use a map of pointers.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Assignment statements

cards.statement: A map range loop visits entries in their insertion order.
cards.explanation: Go leaves map iteration order unspecified and does not guarantee the same order from one iteration to the next.
cards.misconception: Map iteration preserves insertion order.

source.title: Go Blog: Go maps in action

cards.statement: Passing a map to a function gives the function an independent copy of its entries.
cards.explanation: Passing a map copies its reference to the map data. Updates to entries through that parameter affect the caller's map too.
cards.misconception: Passing a map copies its entries into an independent map.

source.title: Effective Go

cards.statement: Goroutines safely read the same map concurrently while updates are absent.
cards.explanation: The FAQ permits concurrent map access when the goroutines are reading. Updates require synchronization with concurrent access.

source.title: Go FAQ

cards.statement: Since Go 1.23, maps.Keys returns a slice containing a map's keys.
cards.explanation: maps.Keys returns an iter.Seq[K] iterator over keys. It does not return a slice.
cards.misconception: maps.Keys returns a collected slice of keys.

source.title: maps package documentation

cards.statement: Two values of `struct{ N int; Label string }` accept comparison with the `==` operator.
cards.explanation: Struct comparison is valid when its field types are comparable, as int and string are.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Comparison operators

cards.statement: For `a` of type `struct{ N int }`, `b := a` makes assignments to `b.N` update `a.N` too.
cards.explanation: Struct assignment copies its directly declared field values. Assigning to b.N leaves a.N unchanged.
cards.misconception: Struct assignment makes the original and destination share their ordinary int fields.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Assignment statements

cards.statement: For a pointer `p` to a struct with field `Name`, `p.Name` accesses the same field as `(*p).Name`.
cards.explanation: Go follows a struct pointer for a field selector, so p.Name abbreviates (*p).Name.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Selectors

cards.statement: For a pointer `p` of type `*int`, `p + 1` advances to the next integer in memory.
cards.explanation: Go rejects pointer addition. The expression p + 1 fails to compile when p has type *int.
cards.misconception: Go permits pointer arithmetic to advance through adjacent values.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Arithmetic operators

cards.statement: A function safely returns `&n` when `n` is an `int` local to that function.
cards.explanation: Taking a local variable's address keeps that variable available to callers that retain the pointer.

source.title: Effective Go: Constructors and composite literals

cards.statement: In the struct type `struct{ *Item }`, Go gives the embedded pointer field the name `Item`.
cards.explanation: Go uses an embedded field's unqualified type name as its field name, even when the declaration uses a pointer.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Struct types

cards.statement: A struct's declared `Name` field takes precedence over a `Name` field reached through embedding.
cards.explanation: The directly declared field has depth zero, so the selector resolves to it rather than a deeper embedded field.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Selectors

cards.statement: When two fields named `Name` tie at the minimum selector depth, `s.Name` picks the first declared.
cards.explanation: A selector with multiple matching fields at its shallowest depth is illegal. Go rejects the ambiguous field access.
cards.misconception: Declaration order resolves a tie between fields at the same minimum selector depth.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Selectors

cards.statement: Embedding a struct type `Inner` in `Outer` makes an `Outer` value assignable to an `Inner` variable.
cards.explanation: An outer struct's type differs from its embedded struct's type. Embedding leaves assignment between these struct types invalid.
cards.misconception: Embedding establishes a subtype relationship that permits assignment to the embedded struct type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Assignability

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, `struct{ Inner }{Name: "Ada"}` is valid when `Inner` is `struct{ Name string }`.
cards.explanation: A promoted field's own name is a valid struct-literal key when reaching that field crosses embedded structs by value.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Struct literals

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, one struct literal accepts an embedded struct key and a key for a field within that struct.
cards.explanation: A struct literal rejects overlapping field keys: naming an embedded struct and one of its promoted fields in that literal is invalid.
cards.misconception: A promoted field key overrides the embedded struct value supplied by another key.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Struct literals

cards.statement: An existing type implements a new `interface{ M() }` when its method set includes `M()`.
cards.explanation: Interface satisfaction depends on method sets, so a type needs no declaration linking it to the interface.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Implementing an interface

cards.statement: The predeclared type `any` creates a distinct interface type alongside `interface{}`.
cards.explanation: any is an alias for interface{}, so the two spellings denote the same type.
cards.misconception: any is a separately defined interface type rather than an alias.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Interface types

cards.statement: An `error` value holding a nil `*MyError` compares equal to a nil `error` interface value.
cards.explanation: An error holding a nil *MyError still has dynamic type *MyError. Its interface value therefore differs from nil.
cards.misconception: A nil pointer stored in an error makes the enclosing interface nil.

source.title: Go FAQ: Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?

cards.statement: Comparing `any(int(3))` with `any(int64(3))` using `==` yields false.
cards.explanation: Interface equality checks dynamic type as well as dynamic value; int and int64 are different dynamic types.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Comparison operators

cards.statement: The comparison `any([]int{1}) == any([]int{1})` returns false.
cards.explanation: Comparing interface values that hold the same non-comparable dynamic type panics. These interface values both hold []int.
cards.misconception: Interfaces holding slices compare unequal instead of triggering a run-time panic.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Comparison operators

cards.statement: For a method interface `I`, `var _ I = (*T)(nil)` checks `*T`'s implementation at compile time.
cards.explanation: Assigning (*T)(nil) to I requires *T to implement I, so the declaration fails to compile if a method is missing; the blank identifier just discards the value.

source.title: Effective Go: Interface checks

cards.statement: A failed single-value type assertion `x.(T)` raises a run-time panic.
cards.explanation: When the stored value fails the asserted type check, a single-value assertion panics during execution.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Type assertions

cards.statement: For `x` of type parameter type `T` constrained by `any`, the expression `x.(int)` compiles.
cards.explanation: A type assertion requires an interface operand rather than an operand of type parameter type. The compiler rejects x.(int) for x of type parameter type T.
cards.misconception: The interface constraint any makes a type parameter itself a valid type assertion operand.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Type assertions

cards.statement: For `x` of type `any`, `case int, string` in `switch v := x.(type)` gives `v` type `any`.
cards.explanation: A case listing several types keeps the switch variable at the guard expression's type, even after a case matches.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Type switches

cards.statement: A type switch accepts `fallthrough` at the end of a case to run the following case body.
cards.explanation: Go rejects fallthrough in a type switch; that statement is restricted to expression-switch cases.
cards.misconception: A type switch permits fallthrough in the same positions as an expression switch.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Type switches

cards.statement: For `type S struct{ N int }`, a method with receiver `s S` changes the caller's S by assigning `s.N`.
cards.explanation: The value receiver s is a copy of the caller's S. Assigning to the declared int field s.N changes that receiver copy.
cards.misconception: A value receiver changes the caller's struct fields directly.

source.title: Go FAQ: Should I define methods on values or pointers?

cards.statement: For an addressable variable t of type T, calling a method with receiver *T as t.M() uses &t.
cards.explanation: Calling `t.M()` uses the shorthand `(&t).M()` when M is a pointer-receiver method and t is addressable.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Calls

cards.statement: An importing package attaches new methods to a receiver base type defined by the imported package.
cards.explanation: A method's receiver base type must be declared in the same package as the method.
cards.misconception: Imported types accept new method declarations from the importing package.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Method declarations

cards.statement: A method declaration accepts a defined pointer type as its receiver base type.
cards.explanation: For a `*T` receiver, T is the base type. A defined pointer type itself is ineligible as a receiver base type.
cards.misconception: A pointer receiver makes a defined pointer type a valid receiver base type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Method declarations

cards.statement: Go chooses among methods with the same name on one base type by their parameter signatures.
cards.explanation: Methods bound to the same receiver base type need distinct non-blank names. Changing parameter types does not create a separate overload.
cards.misconception: Go overloads method names by parameter signature.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Method declarations

cards.statement: `type Alias = T` gives Alias the method set of T, including methods bound to the defined type T.
cards.explanation: An alias denotes the same type as its target, so the target's bound methods remain available through the alias.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Alias declarations

cards.statement: Evaluating a method value x.M saves its receiver for calls made later through that function value.
cards.explanation: A method value evaluates its receiver expression when the value is created and keeps that receiver for later calls.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Method values

cards.statement: The method expression T.M produces a function with the same parameter list as M's ordinary parameters.
cards.explanation: `T.M` produces a function whose first argument is the receiver, followed by M's ordinary arguments.
cards.misconception: A method expression omits the receiver from its function parameter list.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Method expressions

cards.statement: If struct S embeds *T, S's method set includes unambiguous promoted methods with receiver *T.
cards.explanation: Embedding *T brings its promoted pointer-receiver methods into S's method set, including when S is used as a value.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Struct types

cards.statement: With `type T struct{ Base }; type U T`, U retains methods promoted from the embedded Base field.
cards.explanation: Defining U from T preserves the embedded Base field and its method set, so eligible Base methods still promote to U.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Type definitions

cards.statement: A struct type T with a function-valued field M can also have a method M declared on T.
cards.explanation: A struct's non-blank, directly declared field names and bound method names must be distinct. A function-valued field receives no exception.
cards.misconception: A function-valued field permits a same-named method on its struct type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Method declarations

cards.statement: `f == g` is valid for two variables f and g that share the same function type.
cards.explanation: Go permits a function value to be compared with nil. Comparing two function values with == is a compile-time error.
cards.misconception: Function values with matching types support equality comparisons.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Comparison operators

cards.statement: The bare `return` in `func f() (n int) { n = 3; return }` returns the value 3.
cards.explanation: A bare return uses the function's named result parameters. Here, the assignment to n supplies the result returned to the caller.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Return statements

cards.statement: A function receives its `...int` parameter as a value of type `[]int`.
cards.explanation: Inside the function body, a variadic ...int parameter has type []int, so the function handles its arguments as a slice.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Passing arguments to ... parameters

cards.statement: The value returned by a deferred function replaces the enclosing function's own return value.
cards.explanation: Go discards the values returned by a deferred call; those values do not replace the enclosing function's results.
cards.misconception: A deferred call contributes its return value to the enclosing function's results.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Defer statements

cards.statement: A closure invoked after a captured variable changes reads that variable's updated value.
cards.explanation: The closure and its surrounding function share the captured variable, so the closure reads later assignments to that same variable.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Function literals

cards.statement: For an int variable x, `defer f(x)` makes later assignments to x change the argument received by f.
cards.explanation: Executing a defer statement evaluates and saves the call's arguments immediately, so later assignments leave those saved argument values unchanged.
cards.misconception: Deferred calls postpone argument evaluation until the call runs.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Defer statements

cards.statement: When a function returns, Go invokes its deferred calls in reverse registration order.
cards.explanation: Deferred calls run from the most recently scheduled call back to the earliest, immediately before the surrounding function returns.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Defer statements

cards.statement: Go ignores a deferred closure's assignment to a named result after an explicit `return` statement.
cards.explanation: An explicit return sets named result parameters first. A deferred closure can still assign to them before the caller receives the results.
cards.misconception: An explicit return expression fixes a named result before deferred closures run.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Defer statements

cards.statement: A `defer` inside a loop runs its scheduled call when that loop iteration ends.
cards.explanation: Deferred calls run when the surrounding function returns, not when a loop iteration ends, so a defer in a loop body keeps each iteration's call pending until the function exits.
cards.misconception: A loop iteration defines the execution boundary for calls deferred inside it.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Defer statements

cards.statement: Deferring a nil function value causes a panic as the `defer` statement executes.
cards.explanation: Deferring a nil function value succeeds. The panic occurs later, when Go invokes that saved nil function value.
cards.misconception: Registering a deferred nil function call immediately invokes the nil function.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Defer statements

cards.statement: A three-clause for loop accepts a short variable declaration as its post statement.
cards.explanation: Go rejects := in the post position of a three-clause for loop. An assignment or another permitted simple statement belongs there.
cards.misconception: The post statement of a three-clause for loop accepts := declarations.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.22, range `:=` variables get per-iteration scope by default with go.mod go 1.22 or later.
cards.explanation: Range variables declared with := belong to individual iterations when the module declares go 1.22 or later.
cards.appliesTo: Go 1.22 and later (go.mod go 1.22 or later)

source.title: Fixing For Loops in Go 1.22

cards.statement: Since Go 1.22, with go.mod go 1.22 or later, Go copies loop init `:=` variables into new ones before post by default.
cards.explanation: A three-clause loop's next declared variable starts with the previous iteration variable's current value. The post statement then operates on this new variable.
cards.appliesTo: Go 1.22 and later (go.mod go 1.22 or later)

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements

cards.statement: With nil p of type `*struct{ A [3]int }`, the loop `for i := range p.A { _ = i }` evaluates its p.A selector.
cards.explanation: In an index-only range, constant len(p.A) makes Go skip evaluating p.A. The field selector therefore does not dereference the nil p here.
cards.misconception: Range evaluates its expression even when the index-only constant-length exception applies.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements

cards.statement: If f returns a nil *[3]int, the loop `for i := range f() { _ = i }` runs three iterations.
cards.explanation: An index-only range over an array pointer generates indexes from the array length. It does not index the pointed-to array, so its nil pointer is safe here.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements

cards.statement: A range loop over a nil []int slice raises a panic before its first iteration.
cards.explanation: A nil slice contributes zero entries to range, so the loop body runs zero times.
cards.misconception: A nil slice causes range to panic before iteration starts.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.22, ranging over a positive integer n yields integer values from 0 through n-1.
cards.explanation: An integer range uses n as an exclusive upper bound, so its last iteration value is n-1.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.22, `for i := range int64(3)` declares i with type int by default.
cards.explanation: Ranging over a typed integer makes the iteration variable use the bound's type. Here, int64(3) makes i an int64.
cards.misconception: Integer range declares an int iteration variable regardless of the bound's integer type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements

cards.statement: Since Go 1.23, a range loop's yield function panics when an iterator invokes it after it returns false.
cards.explanation: Once yield returns false, that range iteration has stopped. A later call to the same yield function panics.

source.title: iter package: Iterators

cards.statement: Since Go 1.23, iter.Pull's stop function consumes the remaining sequence before ending iteration.
cards.explanation: iter.Pull's stop function ends iteration early. Call it when abandoning a sequence that next has yet to report as finished.
cards.misconception: Stopping a pull iterator drains its remaining sequence.

source.title: iter package: Pull

cards.statement: The Go program continues running after a panic escapes a worker goroutine.
cards.explanation: A panic that escapes a worker goroutine terminates the whole program, even when the panic originates outside main.
cards.misconception: An unrecovered panic ends the worker goroutine while leaving the rest of the Go program running.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Handling panics

cards.statement: Two `errors.New("x")` calls return error values that compare equal with `==`.
cards.explanation: errors.New creates a fresh error value for a call, so equal message text does not make separately created errors equal.
cards.misconception: Matching message text makes separately created errors the same error value.

source.title: errors package: New

cards.statement: The call `fmt.Errorf("read: %v", err)` wraps the error supplied as `err`.
cards.explanation: In fmt.Errorf, %v adds an error's text; %w records the supplied error as a wrapped operand.
cards.misconception: Formatting an error with %v preserves it as a wrapped error.

source.title: fmt package: Errorf

cards.statement: With two error operands, `fmt.Errorf("%w; %w", a, b)` returns an error with `Unwrap() []error`.
cards.explanation: fmt.Errorf with several %w verbs returns an error whose Unwrap method returns the wrapped operands as []error.

source.title: fmt package: Errorf

cards.statement: For an error tree, `errors.Is` checks the root before descending depth-first through its children.
cards.explanation: errors.Is explores one child branch depth-first before checking a sibling branch, after checking the current error.

source.title: errors package: Is

cards.statement: The call `errors.As(errors.New("x"), nil)` raises a run-time panic.
cards.explanation: errors.As needs a non-nil target pointer to an error type or interface. Passing nil for the target with a real error triggers a panic.

source.title: errors package: As

cards.statement: Calling `errors.Join` with two nil error arguments produces a nil `error` result.
cards.explanation: errors.Join discards nil arguments; an input list containing only nil values leaves it with no errors to join.

source.title: errors package: Join

cards.statement: Calling `errors.Unwrap` on an error returned by `errors.Join` returns its first wrapped error.
cards.explanation: errors.Unwrap calls Unwrap() error. A non-nil joined error exposes Unwrap() []error, so errors.Unwrap returns nil for it.
cards.misconception: errors.Unwrap extracts the first child from an error that wraps several errors.

source.title: errors package: Unwrap

cards.statement: A panic runs the deferred calls on the panicking goroutine's call stack as it unwinds.
cards.explanation: During a panic, Go executes the deferred calls belonging to functions affected on that goroutine's stack.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Handling panics

cards.statement: After completed recovery in its deferred function, the enclosing function continues after the panicking call.
cards.explanation: A function containing a recovery defer returns to its caller when recovery completes successfully; its body does not resume at the panic site.
cards.misconception: Recovery resumes the enclosing function's ordinary body immediately after the call that panicked.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Handling panics

cards.statement: Since Go 1.21, `panic(nil)` produces a `*runtime.PanicNilError` panic value by default.
cards.explanation: Go supplies a *runtime.PanicNilError as the panic value, so a valid recover call receives an error value.

source.title: runtime package: PanicNilError

cards.statement: In `go f(g())`, the calling goroutine evaluates g() before f starts in the new goroutine.
cards.explanation: A go statement evaluates and saves the call's arguments in the calling goroutine before starting the invoked function.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Go statements

cards.statement: When main returns, Go keeps the program running until its other goroutines finish.
cards.explanation: Returning from main ends the program. Remaining goroutines do not keep it alive.
cards.misconception: Remaining goroutines keep a Go program alive after main returns.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Program execution

cards.statement: A send on an unbuffered channel completes before a matching receive becomes ready.
cards.explanation: An unbuffered send proceeds when a matching receiver is ready to communicate.
cards.misconception: An unbuffered send finishes before its receiving operation becomes ready.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Send statements

cards.statement: Receiving from a nil channel immediately yields the zero value of its element type.
cards.explanation: A receive from a nil channel blocks forever. The operation has no communication that could make it proceed.
cards.misconception: A nil channel immediately supplies a zero value to a receiver.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Receive operator

cards.statement: A function parameter of type `<-chan int` accepts an argument of type `chan int`.
cards.explanation: Assigning a bidirectional channel to a receive-only channel type narrows the operations permitted through that parameter.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Assignability

cards.statement: Sending a value on a closed channel raises a run-time panic, even if its buffer has free space.
cards.explanation: Closing a channel ends its sending phase. A later send triggers a panic instead of storing the value.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Send statements

cards.statement: The call `close(ch)` type-checks for a parameter ch declared as `<-chan int`.
cards.explanation: close requires a channel whose type permits sends. A receive-only <-chan int channel is rejected at compile time.
cards.misconception: A receive-only channel parameter permits its receiver to close the channel.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Close

cards.statement: The loop `for range ch {}` ends when it receives from ch after closure and after ch's buffer drains.
cards.explanation: The loop receives values until closure and exhaustion of the channel's buffer. An empty open channel makes this loop wait for another value.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements

cards.statement: By default, a select with several ready communication cases chooses the one appearing first in source order.
cards.explanation: select chooses among ready communication cases by uniform pseudo-random selection. Source order provides no priority.
cards.misconception: select chooses its first ready case in source order.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Select statements

cards.statement: A select executes its default branch while its communication cases are blocked.
cards.explanation: The default branch gives select a path to proceed when no channel communication is ready.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Select statements

cards.statement: The expression `len(ch)` reports the number of free buffer slots in a buffered channel ch.
cards.explanation: len(ch) counts values queued in the channel buffer. Free slots are the buffer capacity minus that count.
cards.misconception: The length of a channel measures its unused buffer capacity.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Length and capacity

cards.statement: Go's memory model gives data-race-free programs sequentially consistent behavior.
cards.explanation: A race-free Go program's outcomes match an interleaving of goroutine operations that preserves each goroutine's program order.

source.title: The Go Memory Model

cards.statement: Go preserves slice descriptor consistency during concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes.
cards.explanation: A race on a multiword slice value can expose components from different writes. Such inconsistent pointer and length pairs can cause memory corruption.
cards.misconception: Go preserves the internal consistency of slice values even when goroutines race on them.

source.title: The Go Memory Model

cards.statement: Unlocking a used `sync.Mutex` makes subsequent copies of that mutex safe for synchronization.
cards.explanation: The sync contract prohibits copying a Mutex after its first use; unlocking it does not reset that restriction.
cards.misconception: An unlocked Mutex becomes safe to copy even after earlier use.

source.title: sync package: Mutex

cards.statement: A locked `sync.Mutex` accepts `Unlock` from a goroutine other than the one that locked it.
cards.explanation: A Mutex has no goroutine owner. One goroutine can lock it and arrange for another goroutine to unlock the same mutex.

source.title: sync package: Mutex.Unlock

cards.statement: Calling `sync.RWMutex.Lock` while holding its read lock upgrades that lock to a write lock.
cards.explanation: RWMutex offers no read-to-write lock upgrade. Lock waits for outstanding readers, including the caller's own read lock, to release their locks.
cards.misconception: Calling Lock converts an existing RWMutex read lock into a write lock.

source.title: sync package: RWMutex

cards.statement: A `sync.Once` treats a panic from the function passed to `Do` as a completed invocation.
cards.explanation: If the function passed to Once.Do panics, later Do calls on that Once return without invoking the function again.

source.title: sync package: Once.Do

cards.statement: The `atomic.Int64.Swap` method returns the new value that it stores in the variable.
cards.explanation: atomic.Int64.Swap replaces the stored value atomically and returns the value present before the swap.
cards.misconception: Swap reports the newly stored value instead of the preceding value.

source.title: sync/atomic package: Int64.Swap

cards.statement: Calling a child context's cancel function also cancels the parent context it derives from.
cards.explanation: Calling the cancel function returned for a child context affects that child's cancellation; it leaves the parent's cancellation state unchanged.
cards.misconception: Cancellation of a derived context propagates upward to its parent.

source.title: context package: Cancellation

cards.statement: A caller releases a derived context's cancellation resources by invoking its CancelFunc.
cards.explanation: Calling the CancelFunc removes the parent's reference to the child context and stops associated timers.

source.title: context package: Cancellation

cards.statement: After its cancel function records a `*MyError` cause, a `context.WithCancelCause` context returns it from `Err`.
cards.explanation: Context.Err reports context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded. context.Cause retrieves a separately recorded custom cancellation error.
cards.misconception: A custom cancellation cause replaces the standard error returned by Context.Err.

source.title: context package: WithCancelCause

cards.statement: When `context.AfterFunc` invokes its callback after cancellation, the callback runs in its own goroutine.
cards.explanation: The callback runs in a separate goroutine, including when the context is already canceled at registration.

source.title: context package: AfterFunc

cards.statement: Given `func id[T any](x T) T`, a call written as `id(7)` instantiates id with the type argument int.
cards.explanation: 7 is an untyped constant, so inference uses its default type: with no typed argument for T, the spec infers int, the default type of an integer constant.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Type inference

cards.statement: The type `any` satisfies the `comparable` constraint when supplied as a generic type argument.
cards.explanation: Go's constraint satisfaction exception admits ordinary interface types such as any as comparable type arguments.

source.title: All your comparable types

cards.statement: For `type Count int`, a generic parameter constrained by `~int` accepts Count as its type argument.
cards.explanation: The ~int constraint includes defined types whose underlying type is int, so Count meets this constraint.

source.title: An Introduction To Generics

cards.statement: An interface type declared as `interface{ ~int | ~string }` is a valid type for an ordinary variable.
cards.explanation: An interface containing type terms serves as a constraint; Go rejects it as an ordinary variable's type.
cards.misconception: Constraint interfaces are ordinary variable types.

source.title: An Introduction To Generics

cards.statement: A function constrained by `cmp.Ordered` accepts complex128 as its type argument.
cards.explanation: cmp.Ordered includes integer, floating-point and string types. Complex types fall outside its type set.
cards.misconception: Complex types satisfy cmp.Ordered.

source.title: cmp package: Ordered

cards.statement: `interface{ int | int }` is a legal type constraint for the type parameter of a generic function.
cards.explanation: Non-interface union terms need disjoint type sets. Repeating int makes this constraint illegal.
cards.misconception: Union constraints accept repeated non-interface terms.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: General interfaces

cards.statement: Since Go 1.26, `type Merger[T Merger[T]] interface{ Merge(T) T }` is a valid generic type declaration.
cards.explanation: A generic type's parameter constraint can refer to that generic type, as Merger[T] does in this declaration.

source.title: Go 1.26 Release Notes: Changes to the language

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, `func (s Set[T]) Map[U any](f func(T) U) []U` is a valid signature for `type Set[T any] []T`.
cards.explanation: Map declares its own U in addition to the receiver's T. Its result slice uses U while its function argument accepts T.

source.title: Generic Methods

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, a generic method implements an interface method when an instantiation matches the required signature.
cards.explanation: Interface implementation depends on the type's declared methods. Instantiating a generic method does not make it implement an interface method.
cards.misconception: A matching instantiation of a generic method satisfies an interface method.

source.title: Generic Methods

cards.statement: For `type Box[T any] struct{ V T }`, a method receiver `b Box[U]` uses an existing type named U.
cards.explanation: The receiver Box[U] declares a method-local type parameter U, with the constraint inherited from Box's corresponding parameter.
cards.misconception: Receiver type arguments refer to existing types.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Method declarations

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, given `func id[T any](x T) T`, the literal `[]func(int) int{id}` infers T as int.
cards.explanation: The composite literal supplies the expected func(int) int element type. Go uses that context to instantiate the generic function.

source.title: Go 1.27 is released

cards.statement: The package-level declaration `var Étage int` exports Étage to importing packages.
cards.explanation: É is a Unicode uppercase letter, so the package-level name Étage is exported.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Exported identifiers

cards.statement: A package-level variable named cache has scope limited to the source file that declares it.
cards.explanation: A variable declared at top level has package-block scope, so every file of the same package can use cache, whatever its case. Imported package names, by contrast, are scoped to the file that imports them.
cards.misconception: A lower-case package-level variable is visible only in the file that declares it.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Declarations and scope

cards.statement: Package `example.com/m/b` successfully imports `example.com/m/a/internal/x` within module `example.com/m`.
cards.explanation: An import of example.com/m/a/internal/x needs an importing path within example.com/m/a. Sharing the outer module is insufficient.
cards.misconception: Sharing a module grants access to its internal packages regardless of the directory above internal.

source.title: go command: Internal packages

cards.statement: Go lets package a import package b when package b already imports package a.
cards.explanation: Go rejects a package importing itself through another package; the resulting import cycle is illegal.
cards.misconception: Packages can import one another in a cycle.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Import declarations

cards.statement: A blank import schedules the imported package's initialization as a dependency.
cards.explanation: A blank import triggers initialization side effects even when code uses none of that package's exported names.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Import declarations

cards.statement: At package level, `var a = b; var b = 7` initializes b before a despite their declaration order.
cards.explanation: The initializer for package-level a reads b, so Go initializes b first despite its later declaration.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Package initialization

cards.statement: The compiler rejects two `func init() {}` declarations placed in one source file.
cards.explanation: Go permits multiple init functions in one source file; each serves as a separate initialization function.
cards.misconception: A source file's init function name follows the ordinary uniqueness rule for function declarations.

source.title: Effective Go: The init function

cards.statement: Since Go 1.21, Go initializes the lexically earliest import path among packages ready for initialization.
cards.explanation: Among packages whose imports are already initialized, Go chooses the earliest import path in sorted order.

source.title: Go 1.21 Release Notes: Changes to the language

cards.statement: Since Go 1.21, the go directive sets an advisory minimum toolchain version for the module.
cards.explanation: The go directive declares a mandatory minimum Go version. A toolchain older than that requirement refuses to use the module.
cards.misconception: The go directive remains an advisory minimum version.

source.title: go.mod file reference: go

cards.statement: Since Go 1.26, `go mod init` with a Go 1.27 toolchain writes `go 1.26.0` into a new go.mod.
cards.explanation: For a released Go 1.N.X toolchain, go mod init writes go 1.(N-1).0. With Go 1.27, that produces go 1.26.0.

source.title: Go 1.26 Release Notes: Go command

cards.statement: A module published at v2.0.0 uses `example.com/m` as its module path.
cards.explanation: For a module released at v2.0.0, the path is example.com/m/v2. Its package import paths use that suffixed module path as their prefix.
cards.misconception: Major version 2 modules keep the unsuffixed module path.

source.title: Go Modules Reference: Major version suffixes
